definitions.meaning: A matter resulting in a potential loss of revenue charged on or by reference to: income arising from a source outside the UK; assets situated or held outside the UK (per TCGA92/S21(1) meaning of 'assets', including physical assets, options, debts, incorporeal property, and currency including sterling); activities carried on wholly or mainly outside the UK; or anything having effect as if it were such income, assets or activities. A failure to notify that does not involve an offshore matter but is deliberate (concealed or not), results in potential lost revenue in income tax or CGT, and meets the applicable condition of Para 6AA - i.e., income or proceeds (or part) are received in or transferred before the calculation date to a territory outside the UK. definitions.meaning: Occurs when a person gives HMRC a document they know contains an inaccuracy; it is not necessary that they knew the correct figure, only that the figure given was known to be wrong. No additional steps are taken to hide the inaccuracy.

note.summary: This chunk defines and gives examples of 'deliberate but not concealed' and 'deliberate and concealed' inaccuracies under the FA07/SCH24 penalty regime for inaccurate documents. A deliberate inaccuracy requires only that the person knew the figure given to HMRC was wrong, not that they knew the correct figure. Concealment additionally requires active steps to hide the inaccuracy, such as false invoices, backdated contracts, false records or destroyed books. Worked examples (including a Self Assessment hairdresser case, Mary) illustrate how officers distinguish the two categories, and the manual notes HMRC may refer the most serious cases for criminal investigation despite penalties being civil.

note.summary: This chunk explains the special Schedule 24 FA2007 rules for calculating potential lost revenue (PLR) where an inaccuracy is a 'delayed tax' inaccuracy - i.e. a timing-only error where an understatement in one period is closely linked to a later overstatement/reversal. Instead of the normal PLR rules, PLR is calculated as 5% of the delayed tax per year of delay (pro-rata for periods under a year), based on the gap between the period end date of the inaccurate return and the period end date of the return where it was or would be reversed. The provisions apply to careless, deliberate, and deliberate-and-concealed inaccuracies, but not to wrongly recorded losses or inheritance tax, and not where unrelated errors exist in the same period. Several worked VAT examples illustrate the calculation.

note.summary: This chunk explains HMRC's repayment interest rules under FA 2009, covering when interest starts and ends on overpaid tax. Rule 2 applies to amounts not yet paid to HMRC but arising from a return/claim (currently only VAT from 01/01/2023), running from the later of the required filing date or actual filing date. It covers grouping inaccuracies with the same behaviour and disclosure type to simplify PLR/penalty calculation, when grouping is not permitted (different behaviours, disclosure types, offshore categories, or misaligned suspension conditions), the required order for calculating PLR across increasing rate bands (careless, then deliberate, then deliberate and concealed), and how overstatements must be set against understatements starting with the least serious behaviour so the most serious retains the highest tax rate. It also defines an overstatement and notes that further reliefs/allowances claimed during a compliance check are not treated as overstatements for PLR purposes, while omitted amounts required by law or commercial accounting principles are.

caveats: These special avoidance-arrangement reasonable care rules apply only where the inaccuracy is in a return/document submitted on or after 16 November 2017 relating to a tax period that began on or after 6 April 2017 and ended after 15 November 2017; otherwise the normal reasonable care rules in CH81120 apply.

The presumption of carelessness for avoidance-related inaccuracies can be displaced either by the person proving reasonable care or, conversely, is not needed if HMRC instead proves the inaccuracy was deliberate (a different, more serious behaviour category with its own burden of proof on HMRC).

Advice otherwise disqualified under grounds 1-3 (interested person, arrangement with interested person, lack of appropriate expertise) is not disqualified if P took reasonable steps and reasonably believed it would not be disqualified - a fact-specific exception.
The 'interested person' final-bullet exception additionally requires that Condition E (but none of Conditions A-D) of Sch24 FA2007 para 3B(5) is met, which is a narrow and technical carve-out.
cross_references: Counter Avoidance Technical Advice web page

definitions.meaning: Arrangements (agreement, understanding, scheme, transaction or series of transactions, whether or not legally enforceable) where, having regard to all circumstances, it would be reasonable to conclude that obtaining a tax advantage was the main purpose or one of the main purposes; excludes arrangements in accord with established practices that HMRC had indicated acceptance of at the time entered into. Objective test focused on the main purpose of the arrangements, not of any particular party.

Includes relief/increased relief from tax, repayment/increased repayment of tax, avoidance/reduction of a tax charge or assessment, avoidance of a possible assessment, deferral of payment or advancement of repayment, avoidance of an obligation to deduct/account for tax, and (for VAT) anything within paragraph 5 of Schedule 18 FA2016.
Has the same meaning as paragraph 25 in Part 4 of Schedule 18 to FA 2016.

Advice is disqualified if given by an 'interested person'; given under an arrangement between an interested person and the advisor; given by an advisor without 'the appropriate expertise'; given without regard to P's 'individual circumstances'; or given/addressed to someone other than P. Exceptions apply where P took 'reasonable steps' to identify disqualification and reasonably believed it did not apply, and further exceptions under Sch24 FA2007 para 3B(5) Conditions A-E for the 'interested person' final bullet.

Assessed by considering relevant qualifications, membership of an accredited professional body, whether the advisor's principal business is giving tax advice, and other relevant professional experience; non-exhaustive, case-by-case.

Advice must address the person's specific circumstances rather than being generic advice offered to everybody; consider whether advice only analyses legislation without applying it to the individual's tax affairs.

Basic checks expected of P to identify whether advice was disqualified, e.g. researching the advisor, checking websites, obtaining a trusted independent (e.g. tax professional) view, asking about qualifications/experience, judged against the individual's abilities and circumstances.

Any person other than P who participated in the avoidance arrangement(s) or any transaction forming part of them, or any person who received money/consideration for facilitating P's entry into the arrangement(s); advice from the last category is not disqualified if the advisor had appropriate expertise, took account of P's individual circumstances, and Condition E (but not Conditions A-D) of Sch24 FA2007 para 3B(5) is met.
The arrangements are DOTAS arrangements within the meaning given in FA2014 section 219(5) and (6).
The arrangements are disclosable VAT arrangements or disclosable indirect tax arrangements for the purposes of FA2016 Schedule 18 para 8A to 9A.
P has been given notice that a tax advantage from the arrangement is to be counteracted, and that advantage has been counteracted under FA2013 section 209.

P has been given a follower notice under FA2014 section 204 by reference to the arrangement, and either necessary corrective action has been taken under FA2014 section 208 or the denied advantage has otherwise been counteracted.
A tax advantage asserted by reference to the arrangement has been counteracted on the basis that an avoidance-related rule applies to P's affairs.

note.summary: These pages set out special reasonable care rules for inaccuracies in returns/documents linked to avoidance arrangements, applying to all taxes where the return/document is submitted on or after 16 November 2017 and relates to a tax period beginning on or after 6 April 2017 and ending after 15 November 2017. Where an inaccuracy arises from avoidance arrangements, behaviour is presumed careless unless the inaccuracy was deliberate or the person satisfies HMRC/tribunal they took reasonable care; the burden is on the person (P) to show reasonable care, while HMRC bears the burden of proving deliberate behaviour. Reliance on professional advice can normally show reasonable care, but certain 'disqualified advice' (from interested persons, without appropriate expertise, ignoring individual circumstances, or addressed to someone other than P) cannot be relied on, subject to exceptions for reasonable steps and for certain counteraction scenarios (Conditions A-E). 'Avoidance arrangements' are defined as arrangements where obtaining a tax advantage was a main purpose, tested objectively, excluding arrangements in line with HMRC-accepted established practice.

It explains that normal salary/dividends do not count as personal gain, that apportionment decisions are generally irreversible, and sets out officers' limited appeal rights against PLNs. A final section addresses how VAT/excise wrongdoing penalties interact with other penalties or surcharges on the same tax liability, requiring reduction (but not below zero) to avoid double penalisation.

It explains how tax-geared penalties are calculated using best estimate of liability when a return remains unfiled, how disclosure can reduce the 70%/100% penalties but not the 5% penalty, and the process for calculating each penalty type. Penalties can be amended once actual liability is known, and taxpayers retain appeal rights even against determination-based penalty assessments.

It defines how potential lost revenue (PLR) is calculated for each failure type and introduces the penalty percentage framework based on behaviour (deliberate/concealed, deliberate, non-deliberate) and quality of disclosure (telling, helping, giving access), plus the distinction between prompted and unprompted disclosure. While framed around VAT and other duties, the general failure-to-notify penalty architecture (PLR, disclosure quality, prompted/unprompted) is the same regime referenced elsewhere for income tax/CGT failure-to-notify cases relevant to Self Assessment registration obligations.

note.summary: This chunk sets out how HMRC calculates Potential Lost Revenue (PLR) for failure-to-notify penalties under FA08/Sch41. General rules state PLR is the unpaid tax/duty resulting from the failure, excluding overpayments by other persons unless their liability is directly adjustable by reference to the defaulter's liability. Specific rules are given for Income Tax/CGT (PLR = tax unpaid at 31 January following the tax year, or later dates if a notice to file was withdrawn), Corporation Tax (PLR = tax unpaid 12 months after the accounting period end, including certain loans-to-participators liabilities), and VAT registration (PLR = VAT due for the period from when registration should have occurred to when HMRC became aware, less certain EU-tax deductions). Worked examples illustrate each calculation.
